title: An Integrated Explainable Machine Learning Framework for Cell-to-Pack Imbalance Prediction in Electric Vehicle Battery Systems
abstract: This study presents a machine learning framework for predicting cell-to-pack imbalance in electric vehicle batteries. A set of battery attributes that affect battery performance, including State of Charge (SOC), State of Health (SOH), temperature (including ambient temperature and humidity), and cabin temperature, were used to make this prediction. The collected battery data were pre-processed to improve prediction performance. Three preprocessing methods were used: (i) Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD); (ii) deep denoising autoencoders, and (iii) feature selection using minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance (mRMR) mutual information. This preprocessing step removes noise from the dataset and identifies useful information for prediction. Cell-to-pack imbalance prediction was performed using three interpretable machine learning models: (i) an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM); (ii) fuzzy regression; and (iii) RuleFit. These models provide transparent predictions and help in understanding the factors responsible for battery imbalance. Models were evaluated on an independent 20-sample test set held out from the 100-record dataset. Among the three interpretable models, Fuzzy Regression achieved the strongest predictive performance (R² = 0.998), followed by RuleFit (R² = 0.976), while EBM achieved a lower R² of 0.201 on this independent test set despite providing detailed feature-level explanations. These results indicate that combining signal preprocessing, feature selection, and interpretable regression can provide useful and explainable information for cell-to-pack imbalance prediction, while also showing that performance can vary substantially between interpretable models on a small, two-pack dataset; validation on larger and more varied battery datasets is needed to confirm generalizability.
venue: International Journal of Electrical and Electronics Engineering

title: Degradation-Aware Management of Second-Life Lithium-Ion Banks Using Probabilistic SOH Derating in Isolated Microgrids
abstract: Second-life lithium-ion banks in isolated microgrids combine heterogeneous, partially degraded cells with harsh tropical operation, yet conventional battery management reacts to voltage limits only once they are reached. This work proposes a degradation-aware battery management system in which the probabilistic state-of-health (SOH) estimate of each cell, obtained by Gaussian process regression, sets a proactive current-derating factor through an uncertainty-penalized effective SOH (μ−2σ), so that estimation uncertainty becomes a control variable. The estimator was validated on four public datasets spanning four chemistry/format combinations, including six LG INR21700-M50T cells with a measured 50-month electric-vehicle-to-storage transition (out-of-fold RMSE 0.28% SOH; 0.69–2.29% on NASA, CALCE, and RWTH benchmarks). An independent 36-cell pack dataset confirms the premise: 14 cells fall below 3.0 V while the pack voltage still reads nominal. At the cycle level, the derating removes every envelope violation of unprotected operation while extracting 3.5% more energy than a safe per-cell cutoff. Over 1500 simulated days of an off-grid photovoltaic microgrid in the Colombian non-interconnected zones, with a bank built from the six measured second-life cells, the strategy preserves 6.5 SOH percentage points at zero loss of supply, rising to 11.8 pp at 35 °C and 13.9 pp for a pre-aged bank, where only the managed bank avoids end of life. The control law is algebraic (∼2 μs per evaluation), computationally compatible with low-cost embedded implementation.
title_zh: Degradation-Aware Management of Second-Life Lithium-Ion Banks Using Probabilistic SOH Derating in Isolated Microgrids

title: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives in Thermal Runaway Prevention and Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Widespread deployment of lithium-ion batteries in energy storage and transportation increases the need to prevent and control thermal runaway and associated hazards. Focusing on energy storage systems using lithium iron phosphate batteries while drawing on other battery chemistries, this review examines failure mechanisms, hazard evolution, mitigation technologies, and engineering applicability. It analyzes coupled interfacial reactions, material transformations, and structural failure, alongside the effects of chemistry, state of charge, capacity, and aging. Multisignal warning and intervention, passive thermal barriers, active fire suppression and cooling, and combined strategies are compared in terms of mechanisms and operating conditions. Engineering assessment addresses experimental comparability, maturity, scalability, cost, and environmental safety. The synthesis identifies flame extinguishment, cell thermal stabilization, and propagation prevention as distinct objectives requiring complementary indicators. Warning effectiveness depends on timely intervention, whereas barrier–cooling integration depends on heat-transfer pathways, agent accessibility, and sustained supply. Technology selection therefore requires validation at the intended scale under relevant application constraints. Future priorities include linking warning to intervention, integrating barriers with sustained cooling, and developing evaluation frameworks with clearly defined applicability. Engineering validation should also incorporate long-term reliability, life-cycle costs, environmental impacts, and personnel safety to support application-specific mitigation strategies.
title_zh: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives in Thermal Runaway Prevention and Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries
